$comment: California entity obligations. These attach to any company doing business in California, whether or not it was formed there — which is the case that surprises Delaware-incorporated founders operating out of California.

clauses.title: California Annual Tax and Fee
clauses.rationale: Owed on doing business in California regardless of where the entity was formed and regardless of profit. Founders who form in Delaware and operate from California routinely budget for Delaware franchise tax and are surprised by this one.
clauses.body: California charges a [[franchise tax]] of {{caAnnualTax}}. This is owed for doing business in California whether or not the Company was formed here and whether or not it made money. An LLC additionally owes {{caLlcFeeTiers}}, estimated on Form 3536 by the fifteenth day of the sixth month and trued up on the return. The gross receipts fee is computed on total California income, not on profit, so a low-margin business can owe it while operating at a loss.

clauses.title: California Statement of Information
clauses.rationale: Separate from the formation filing and from the tax return, which is why it is the filing most often missed. Suspension is the consequence, and a suspended entity cannot enforce its own contracts.
clauses.body: California requires an entity to file the initial Statement of Information with the Secretary of State within ninety (90) days after the original articles are filed, and {{caSoiRenewal}} thereafter for a {{entityLong}} — annually for a corporation, biennially for a limited liability company. The filing period is not a date: it is the calendar month in which the original articles were filed together with the immediately preceding five calendar months. The Secretary of State sends a reminder about three months before that period closes, and failing to receive it is not an excuse. On a failure to file, the Secretary of State first gives notice of delinquency; only if no statement is filed within sixty (60) days of that notice is the entity certified to the Franchise Tax Board, which then assesses a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250). The Secretary of State may waive the penalty for reasonable cause or unusual circumstances that justify the failure, and the delinquency notice must say so. For a corporation, suspension is a separate and much later step: it requires a failure to file for the period, no statement filed during the preceding twenty-four (24) months, and certification for penalty for that same period, after which a further sixty-day notice runs before the powers are suspended. While suspended, the corporation's powers, rights and privileges are suspended except for filing an application for exempt status or amending the articles to perfect that application or to set forth a new name, and the practical consequence is that it is disabled from participating in litigation — it can neither prosecute nor defend. The statement may be filed notwithstanding suspension and is what lifts it: the Secretary of State certifies the filing to the Franchise Tax Board and the corporation may then be relieved, unless the Franchise Tax Board holds it suspended for tax reasons. Do not assume the harsher consequences follow from this suspension: contracts made while suspended are voidable by the other party, and the entity's name becomes available to others, under the Revenue and Taxation Code provisions that apply to a Franchise Tax Board suspension for unpaid tax, not under the Corporations Code provision that applies to a missed Statement of Information.

defects: The LLC suspension path was not fully traced. §17713.09 gives the LLC delinquency, certification and penalty route and it matches §2204 almost word for word, but no LLC counterpart to §2205's suspension mechanism was read. The rebuilt body states the suspension sequence for corporations only. An LLC reader is told the penalty route and no suspension route, which is narrower than the law may be and is deliberately narrow rather than guessed.
Whether a suspended LLC suffers the same litigation disability as a suspended corporation was not verified and is not asserted.

clauses.title: Fictitious Business Name
clauses.rationale: A county filing, not a state one, so it is easy to overlook after completing the Secretary of State paperwork. Without it the company cannot sue on a contract made under the trade name.
clauses.body: If the Company operates under any name other than {{company}}, file a [[fictitious business name]] statement with the county clerk where its principal place of business sits, within forty (40) days of first transacting business under that name, and publish it once a week for four (4) successive weeks. The statement expires after five (5) years. Until it is filed, the Company cannot maintain an action on a contract made under the trade name.

clauses.title: Seller's Permit and Sales Tax
clauses.rationale: Required before the first sale, not after, and personal liability for unremitted sales tax reaches responsible individuals directly.
clauses.body: California requires a seller of tangible goods to register with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration for a [[seller's permit]] before making the first sale of tangible goods. Collect and remit sales tax on the schedule assigned, and track district taxes, which vary by delivery location rather than by the seller's address. Unremitted sales tax can be assessed personally against responsible individuals, and that liability survives dissolution of the entity.

clauses.title: Local Business License
clauses.rationale: California has no statewide business licence, so the obligation is municipal and is triggered by a home office as readily as by a storefront.
clauses.body: California cities generally require a business licence or tax certificate from every California city where the Company has a place of business, including a founder's or remote employee's home office. Several cities tax gross receipts rather than charging a flat fee, and a few assess based on payroll. Renew annually; unpaid municipal business taxes accrue penalties and interest and can block permits.

clauses.title: California LLC Statutory Defaults
clauses.rationale: California's LLC act supplies defaults that differ from what founders assume — including per-capita rather than pro-rata voting on some matters — and it makes a short list of terms non-waivable.
clauses.body: Where this {{govDoc}} is silent, the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act supplies the rule, and several of its defaults differ from common expectation. A short list of provisions cannot be varied by agreement at all, including the duty of loyalty in substance, the obligation of good faith and fair dealing, and a Member's right to information. Provisions in <<xr:gov_voting>> and <<xr:gov_fiduciary>> are written to displace the defaults where displacement is permitted.

clauses.title: California Charging Order
clauses.rationale: California's charging order protection is weaker than Texas's — foreclosure is available on a showing that distributions will not satisfy the judgment within a reasonable time.
clauses.body: A [[charging order]] is a judgment creditor's remedy against a Member's economic interest. California protection is narrower than in some states: a court may order foreclosure of the charged interest where it finds that distributions will not pay the judgment within a reasonable time. Foreclosure transfers economic rights only; the purchaser does not become a Member or acquire management rights.

clauses.title: Section 2115 Pseudo-Foreign Corporation
clauses.rationale: The most commonly overlooked consequence of the Delaware-incorporated, California-operated structure. Incorporating in Delaware does not by itself escape California corporate law.
clauses.body: [[Section 2115|section 2115]] applies core provisions of California corporate law to a corporation incorporated elsewhere when, for the latest fiscal year, more than half of its property, payroll, and sales are in California and more than half of its voting shares are held of record by California residents. The Company is incorporated in {{formStateLong}} and operates in {{opStateLong}}, so the test may apply. Where it does, California rules govern cumulative voting in director elections, director removal, distributions and dividends, dissenters' rights, indemnification limits, and inspection rights — regardless of what the {{charterDoc}} or <<xr:gov_board>> provide. Corporations listed on a major exchange are excluded. Test this annually rather than at formation, because the answer changes as the company grows.

clauses.title: California Professional Practice Restrictions
clauses.rationale: An LLC cannot render licensed professional services in California at all, and the corporate practice of medicine doctrine separately restricts who may own a medical practice.
clauses.body: California does not permit a limited liability company to render professional services requiring a licence. Licensed services must be delivered through a professional corporation or a registered limited liability partnership, with ownership restricted to licensees in the same or a statutorily permitted related profession. For medical services the corporate practice doctrine additionally bars a lay-owned entity from employing physicians or controlling clinical judgment; the usual structure is a management services organization contracting with a professional corporation. Confirm the licence status of every intended service line before filing, as required by <<xr:charter_ca_professional>>.

clauses.title: California Dissolution and Final Returns
clauses.rationale: The annual tax keeps accruing until the entity is formally dissolved, so simply stopping operations does not stop the liability.
clauses.body: Ceasing operations does not end California tax liability. The {{caAnnualTax}} continues to accrue until the Company files a certificate of dissolution or cancellation with the Secretary of State and a final return with the Franchise Tax Board. Dissolve formally and promptly, following the process in <<xr:gov_dissolution>>, rather than allowing the entity to lapse.
